item.title: A Balanced Parametrization of Correlation Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2610.14511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the balanced correlation parametrization (BCP), which maps positive-definite correlation matrices one-to-one onto the set of symmetric hollow matrices. A key feature of the parametrization is that both the transformation and its inverse are available in closed form. It combines marginal and partial correlations, is inverse-consistent and equivariant under variable permutations and sign changes, and preserves block structure. A novel property of BCP is that it preserves correlation sparsity as the dimension tends to infinity under suitable factor conditions, providing a basis for sparse high-dimensional correlation modeling. An empirical illustration using standardized idiosyncratic daily stock returns for 1,765 equities over 15 years shows that BCP retains the approximate sparsity pattern and magnitudes of shock correlations, and that it yields accurate positive-definite reconstructions under sparse coordinate restrictions.
item.dc:creator: Peter Reinhard Hansen, Chen Tong

item.title: Randomized Experiments with Ambiguous Record Linkage
item.description: arXiv:2610.15063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Randomized experiments are often linked to administrative data to measure outcomes, but coarse identifiers can leave multiple administrative records consistent with each experimental unit. We show that unbiased estimation of the sample average treatment effect is possible without resolving these ambiguous links or specifying an outcome model. Our key linkage requirement is that the true administrative outcome is contained among the candidate outcomes for each experimental unit. We characterize the precision cost of linkage ambiguity and study two complementary ways to mitigate it: regression adjustment and reweighting based on observed linkage characteristics. We establish finite-sample and asymptotic properties of these estimators and develop valid randomization-based and large-sample inference.
item.dc:creator: Bruno Ferman, Lucas Finamor

item.title: GMM under finite-population asymptotics: instrumental variables and regression adjustment
item.description: arXiv:2610.15168v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper extends the finite-population asymptotic framework of Abadie et al. (2014,2020) to the generalized method of moments (GMM) estimator for moment condition models. Motivating examples include instrumental variable regressions and regression adjustments under randomized controlled trials. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the GMM estimator and propose conservative variance estimators. We also study GMM weighting, misspecification, and over-identification testing under finite-population asymptotics. Notably, even though the optimally weighted GMM estimator is infeasible under finite-population asymptotics, the regression adjustment estimator in a randomized controlled trial is shown to be asymptotically equivalent to the optimally weighted GMM estimator. A simulation study and real data application illustrate the usefulness of our GMM theory.
item.dc:creator: Haruo Kakehi, Yukitoshi Matsushita, Taisuke Otsu

item.title: Recurrent Neural Networks for Forecasting Autoregressive Noncausal Processes
item.description: arXiv:2610.15296v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper examines the use of recurrent neural networks and their extensions for forecasting autoregressive causal-noncausal processes, characterized by local explosive patterns such as bubbles and spikes. We study the recurrent neural networks (RNN), long short-term memory networks (LSTM), gated recurrent unit (GRU), bidirectional LSTM, and also a simple feed-forward network (FNN) to reveal the difficulty of forecasting extreme values depending on the type of network and the length of the training set. We show that FNN outperforms other networks in predicting extreme values of a univariate noncausal time series during a bubble. We also examine the improvements of point predictions of extreme values resulting from pooling and a modified loss function.
item.dc:creator: Joann Jasiak, Cheng Zhong

item.title: Uncertainty in Compound Decisions
item.description: arXiv:2610.15672v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers and policymakers frequently make a large number of decisions simultaneously over many units using noisy estimates of unit-level effects. Researchers often assume that unit-level effects are drawn from a common effect distribution, allowing for optimal decision-making. In applications, however, this effect distribution is unknown to the econometrician, introducing uncertainty in the ultimate decision-making problem. This paper considers the problem of quantifying this uncertainty. For instance, researchers may seek to understand how an oracle decision maker with knowledge of the effect distribution would compare different feasible decisions, or understand which decisions an oracle would plausibly make. Analyzing these questions from the perspective of an oracle decision maker involves comparing the conditional means of unit-level effects given estimates thereof, suggesting a sufficient inferential objective of uniform coverage of these conditional means. Based on an equivalence between uniform coverage of conditional means and multiple testing, I develop methods that satisfy this coverage. Finally, I consider an application to the problem of identifying high-economic-mobility neighborhoods. My methods sharpen inference relative to existing methods and identify units that can be confidently included in oracle selections.
item.dc:creator: Andreas Petrou-Zeniou

item.title: Estimation of Rational Inattention--Additive Random Utility Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.16701v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops likelihood-based estimation for parametric rational inattention--additive random utility models. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the exact maximum likelihood estimator and provide conditions under which the simulated estimator shares its asymptotic distribution. To implement estimation, we develop Newton--BA, a KKT-guided hybrid of Newton--Raphson and Blahut--Arimoto (BA). The algorithm accommodates both interior and boundary solutions and substantially improves computational efficiency relative to direct BA while preserving numerical accuracy. Monte Carlo simulations show that parameter recovery improves with sample size and that confidence-interval coverage is generally close to the nominal $95$ percent level. Finally, we compare our model with no- and perfect-information logit benchmarks in an empirically calibrated ModeCanada experiment. Our model achieves similar in-sample likelihood fit to perfect-information logit but more accurately recovers key preference parameters, choice probabilities, and responses to travel-time changes.
item.dc:creator: Ruolei Zhu

item.title: Pseudo-Panel Event Studies: Econometric Foundations for Credible Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.16754v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Event studies with panel data are widely used to estimate treatment effects. With repeated cross-sections, future treatment dates are unobserved for untreated individuals. Pseudo-panel event studies impute pre-treatment outcomes of the treated using matched untreated individuals. This paper establishes identification in such designs and characterizes bias when identification conditions fail. I show that the pseudo-panel regression is equivalent to weighted least squares with group means. This representation simplifies computation and yields analytical inference. In simulations, analytical confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage, whereas conventional intervals substantially undercover. I also develop a doubly robust estimator using richer covariates, a symmetric matching design with synthetic type fixed effects, and a fully nonparametric estimator that accommodates heterogeneous treatment effects. In a Korean panel survey, the pseudo-panel regression yields an employment child penalty of 42.1%, close to 46.9% in the actual panel. Applications to repeated cross-sections yield employment penalties of about one-third.
item.dc:creator: Dongwoo Kim

item.title: Dynamic Panel Multinomial Logit Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.17104v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper provides moment conditions for dynamic multinomial logit panel data models with individual specific fixed effects. The moment conditions do not depend on the fixed effects and thus form the basis for generalized method of moments estimation. For a leading case, we provide sufficient conditions under which the moment conditions identify the common parameters, and we illustrate their use in an empirical application to household soft drink purchases. The construction of moment conditions is based on transformed models obtained by permuting outcomes across time periods. For any cyclic permutation, the ratio of the transformed model probability to the true model probability is free of the fixed effects, and comparing two such ratios yields restrictions on the common parameters of interest. This construction is not specific to the multinomial logit. It applies to any dynamic panel data model whose static counterpart admits a symmetric sufficient statistic for the fixed effects. This unifies our main result with analogous results for other models.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Dano, Bo E. Honor\'e, Martin Weidner

item.title: Inference on the Value of Policy Improvement in Adaptive Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2610.15789v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we develop an asymptotically normal estimator for the value of policy improvement (VPI) under adaptively collected data. This value, which is defined as the gap between the value of the best treatment policy in a class and that of a baseline policy, gauges whether or not it is worth deploying a personalized treatment policy. Building an estimator for the VPI is naturally more difficult than estimating the value of a fixed policy. This is because, in addition to contending with the correlated data and decaying propensities associated with adaptive experiments, any estimator must also handle the non-regularity, or lack of pathwise differentiability, of the underlying estimand when the optimal policy is non-unique. Our proposed estimator works by sequentially fitting a weighted empirical welfare maximizing policy on historical data and then evaluating it using inverse propensity weighting on future samples. We neither assume that the optimal policy is unique nor make a margin assumption on the underlying heterogeneous treatment effects. A key difficulty in analyzing our estimator is showing that the regret incurred through policy learning is asymptotically smaller than the standard error of the estimator. We accomplish this by showing faster regret rates for policy learning under decaying propensities, which may be of independent interest. We not only evaluate the coverage of our estimator on a mix of synthetic and semi-synthetic data, but also employ it to estimate the VPI in an adaptive experiment evaluating the efficacy of job assistance programs in Jordan due to Caria et al. Although our estimates are generally more conservative than their hierarchical Bayesian analysis, which assumes that the optimal policy is unique, we still corroborate the benefits of personalization amongst Syrian refugees.
item.dc:creator: Justin Whitehouse, Emma Brunskill, Vasilis Syrgkanis

item.title: Honest Inference for High-Dimensional Linear Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.16503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a heteroskedasticity-robust and dimention-adaptive test for multiple linear restric- tions in sparse high-dimensional linear regression models. It combines desparsified LASSO estimation with a ridge-regularized quadratic form statistic and critical values that adapt to the restriction dimension. Under stated regularity conditions, our approach is asymptotically valid under a fixed or diverging number of restrictions without specifying the asymptotic regime in advance. Our random-design theory allows independent non-identically distributed covari- ate rows with marginal sub-Weibull tails and heteroskedastic errors satisfying finite polynomial moments. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate improved finite-sample size control relative to conventional Wald tests, particularly as the number of restrictions increases.
item.dc:creator: Dennis Lim, Pengjin Min, Jonathan H. W. Tan, Jiezheng Wei

item.title: Risk Measures for the Climate Transition Age: Why Symmetric Risk Budgets are unlikely to mitigate two-dimensionally asymmetric Climate Change risks
item.description: arXiv:2610.18387v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The most widely used investment risk measures - variance, standard deviation, and tracking error - treat upside deviations as equally undesirable as downside losses. In stable markets with assumed symmetric return distributions, this simplification is potentially harmless. In the climate transition age, it is not. Climate risk is two-dimensionally asymmetric, across assets and over time. Both dimensions are negatively skewed against investors. Hence, climate transition investment strategies deliberately deviate from benchmarks that reflect an insufficiently decarbonising global economy. When fiduciaries enforce tracking error budgets that penalise outperformance just as heavily as underperformance, they inadvertently constrain exactly the portfolio return opportunities that climate-aware investing seeks. We argue that replacing symmetric deviation-based risk measures with their downside-only counterparts - semi-variance, standard risk and trailing error - resolves this conflict without sacrificing any fiduciary discipline. The distinction is not merely semantic: as the gap between climate transition trajectories and market benchmarks widens over the coming decades, symmetric risk budgets will become binding constraints on transition strategies well before actual investment risk warrants it. We propose specific changes to mandate design that would allow institutional investors to pursue climate transition opportunities within genuinely risk-aware (rather than deviation-averse) frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Lars Dijkstra, Andreas G. F. Hoepner, Fabiola I. Schneider, Agnieszka S{\l}omka-Go{\l}\k{e}biowska

item.title: Testing for an Explosive Bubble using High-Frequency Volatility
item.description: arXiv:2405.02087v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Based on a continuous-time stochastic volatility model with a linear drift, we develop a test for explosive behavior in financial asset prices at a low frequency when prices are sampled at a higher frequency. The test exploits the volatility information in the high-frequency data. The method consists of devolatizing log-asset price increments with realized volatility measures and performing a supremum-type recursive Dickey-Fuller test on the devolatized sample. The proposed test has a nuisance-parameter-free asymptotic distribution and is easy to implement. We study the size and power properties of the test in Monte Carlo simulations. A real-time date-stamping strategy based on the devolatized sample is proposed for the origination and conclusion dates of the explosive regime. Conditions under which the real-time date-stamping strategy is consistent are established. The test and the date-stamping strategy are applied to study explosive behavior in cryptocurrency and stock markets.
item.dc:creator: H. Peter Boswijk, Jun Yu, Yang Zu

item.title: Maximum score and non-smooth M-estimators with multiway dependence
item.description: arXiv:2604.10232v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Under i.i.d. sampling, the maximum score estimator of Manski (1975) converges at the cube-root rate to a non-Gaussian limit. We show that, under multiway dependence and low-level conditions, it is asymptotically normal at a parametric rate in the smallest number of clusters and, when the cluster-level variance is non-degenerate, as fast as regular estimators such as probit. The result rests on a general theory for non-smooth M-estimators, under which a modified bootstrap is first-order valid given a consistent Hessian estimate. With two-way clustering, a cube-root term can remain; under high-level conditions, symmetric bootstrap intervals for suitable scalar parameters still control size uniformly.
item.dc:creator: Harold D. Chiang, Ahnaf Rafi

item.title: Higher-Order Neyman Orthogonality in Moment-Condition Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.10842v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We construct moment functions that are Neyman-orthogonal to a chosen order in parametric moment condition models involving nuisance parameters. These moment functions reduce sensitivity to estimation error in the nuisance parameters and, as such, offer a unified and tractable route to higher-order debiasing in a wide range of econometric models. The number of additional nuisance parameters required by our construction, beyond those already present in the original moment conditions, is independent of the order of orthogonalization and can be reduced to a single scalar if desired.
item.dc:creator: St\'ephane Bonhomme, Koen Jochmans, Whitney K. Newey, Martin Weidner

item.title: Designing Persuasive Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2605.16703v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Incentives in experimental design are often misaligned: experimenters design and finance experiments to seek regulatory approval, while regulators seek to maximize social welfare. This incentive misalignment is especially relevant for Bayesian and adaptive trial designs, which have gained substantial popularity in recent years and have been actively encouraged by the US Food and Drug Administration. We propose a framework to resolve this conflict, wherein regulators set a minimum welfare threshold, and experimenters optimize designs subject to this constraint. It requires no knowledge of experimenters' private preferences or costs and mitigates strategic Bayesian persuasion. By varying the welfare threshold, we can map the Pareto frontier between the experimenter's and regulator's welfare. Under normal priors, Neyman allocation is always the optimal sampling strategy, regardless of specific objectives. We also characterize the optimal stopping rule. A numerical study calibrated to clinical trial data shows sample size reductions of over 48% relative to classical designs attaining the same social welfare.
item.dc:creator: Karun Adusumilli, Abhi Vemulapati

item.title: Representation Multiplicity in Causal Forests
item.description: arXiv:2609.12406v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Including covariates alongside strictly monotone transformations can change a causal forest's treatment decisions without adding information. Random feature selection favors covariates represented by these multiple columns. Under stated conditions, I show that this imbalance can persist as samples grow. Treatment effect components associated with other covariates are omitted, attenuated, or recovered depending on their inclusion probabilities and tree depth. Simulations and a job-training replication illustrate sensitivity to redundant transformations. Sampling groups of variables that generate identical splits restores prediction invariance on the grouping data when fitting and randomization are held fixed.
item.dc:creator: Yi Niu

item.title: Identification and Inference in proxy-SVARs with non-Gaussian shocks
item.description: arXiv:2609.14398v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two frequent approaches for identifying structural VARs are external instruments, which carry economic content but are often weak, and non-Gaussianity of the shocks, which provides statistical identification but carries no economic meaning. We combine the two strategies in a single generalized method of moments framework. This hybrid approach point-identifies the target shocks while also identifying the non-target shocks up to sign and ordering. Under suitable rank conditions, the higher-order moments of the structural shocks anchor the identification uniformly over the instrument strength. Consequently, under local-to-zero proxy relevance, estimators of the dynamic causal effects remain consistent, and standard asymptotic inference remains valid. Moreover, the Anderson-Rubin confidence sets are substantially narrower than their instrument-only counterparts. The hybrid estimator is also more efficient than either source of identification used in isolation: at any fixed proxy relevance, even a weak instrument increases the efficiency of the estimator through its covariance with the non-Gaussian moment block. Under local deviations from proxy exogeneity, we provide asymptotic bias bounds and show that stronger non-Gaussianity of the shocks compresses the bias. Finally, the over-identified structure yields two mutually orthogonal specification tests for proxy exogeneity and the validity of the higher-order moment conditions. We derive their limiting distributions and provide a bootstrap procedure for finite-sample critical values. Monte Carlo simulations and two applications with identification of oil news-shock and a Euro-area MP shock demonstrate the potential of our framework.
item.dc:creator: Paritosh Shankarrao Junare

item.title: Eigenvalue-Decomposition Cost Denoising for Predict-then-Optimize
item.description: arXiv:2609.15111v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Predict-then-optimize methods learn a mapping from features to unknown edge costs. They then solve the shortest-path problem on the predicted costs. We study a feature-free alternative for the case where the decision-maker observes many noisy cost vectors on a fixed network. The cost vectors are denoised by an eigenvalue decomposition (PCA) of their covariance matrix. Dijkstra's algorithm then runs on the result. We test this on the $5\times5$ grid of \citet{elmachtoub2022}, with $1000$ independent replications and a fresh ground truth in each. We compare against SPO+, against naive Dijkstra on noisy costs, and against two alternatives to a hand-picked rank $k$ (the Gavish-Donoho threshold and a Ledoit-Wolf filter). We also test a hybrid of SPO+ and PCA. Four findings emerge. First, the rank matters. Keeping $k=2$ components performs worse than no denoising. Second, when costs are close to linear in the features, the Gavish-Donoho threshold recovers the true rank without supervision. PCA-denoised Dijkstra outperforms SPO+ at $\deg=1$, but underperforms SPO+ at $\deg\geq 2$. The hybrid works best at $\deg=1$ and is slightly better than SPO+ at $\deg=2$. Third, when costs are strongly nonlinear ($\deg=4$), the signal is no longer low-rank, and only the Ledoit-Wolf filter clearly beats the naive baseline. Fourth, the benefit of denoising grows with network size on grids, but not on a layered non-grid network at high nonlinearity.
item.dc:creator: Henry Aldridge-Krawciw, Irene Aldridge

item.title: Valid Inference After Control Selection in Difference-in-Differences
item.description: arXiv:2610.01464v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop the first empirically implementable selective-inference framework for difference-in-differences with controls selected by pre-treatment fit. We construct confidence intervals for the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), incorporating that selection and estimating the unknown full covariance from the same observations. Counterexamples establish undercoverage from Roth's fixed-comparison pretest adjustment and direct Gaussian-score application of Andrews--Kitagawa--McCloskey to this selection, despite parallel trends for every candidate. Retaining the actual polynomial or piecewise-polynomial event, we establish uniform validity at perfect fit and population ties, endpoint equivalence with known-covariance inference, and unequal-sample guarantees. We accommodate staggered adoption, reused observations, and fitting-rule choice. In police-deployment and minimum-wage reanalyses, we find changes in significance and economically relevant effect ranges while retaining the selected comparison. For a smooth randomized test, we obtain higher-order accuracy through stabilized joint mean--covariance correction preserving normal-sampling baseline rejection probabilities. Researchers should disclose selection rules alongside ATT uncertainty.
item.dc:creator: Takahiro Hoshino, Ryoya Nakano

item.title: Information-Enriched Selection of Stationary and Non-Stationary Autoregressions using the Adaptive Lasso
item.description: arXiv:2402.16580v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a novel approach to elicit the weight of a potentially non-stationary regressor in the consistent and oracle-efficient estimation of autoregressive models using the adaptive Lasso. The enhanced weight builds on a statistic that exploits distinct orders in probability of the OLS estimator in time series regressions when the degree of integration differs. We provide theoretical results on the benefit of our approach for detecting stationarity when a tuning criterion selects the $\ell_1$ penalty parameter. Monte Carlo evidence shows that our proposal is superior to using OLS-based weights, as suggested by Kock [Econom. Theory, 32, 2016, 243-259]. We apply the modified estimator to model selection for German inflation rates after the introduction of the Euro. The results indicate that energy commodity price inflation and headline inflation are best described by stationary autoregressions.
item.dc:creator: Thilo Reinschl\"ussel, Martin C. Arnold

item.title: Bootstrap Adaptive Lasso Solution Path Unit Root Tests
item.description: arXiv:2409.07859v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose sieve wild bootstrap analogues to the adaptive Lasso solution path unit root tests of Arnold and Reinschl\"ussel (2024) arXiv:2404.06205 to improve finite sample properties and extend their applicability to a generalised framework, allowing for non-stationary volatility. Numerical evidence shows the bootstrap to improve the tests' precision for error processes that promote spurious rejections of the unit root null, depending on the detrending procedure. The bootstrap mitigates finite-sample size distortions and restores asymptotically valid inference when the data features time-varying unconditional variance. We apply the bootstrap tests to real residential property prices of the top six Eurozone economies and find evidence of stationarity to be period-specific, supporting the conjecture that exuberance in the housing market characterises the development of Euro-era residential property prices in the recent past.
item.dc:creator: Martin C. Arnold, Thilo Reinschl\"ussel
